old.headline: The Achilles signal from Thursday is the whole story this week — we pull quality out, keep running only if pain stays low and not worsening, and you get it looked at by a sports physio.
old.analysis:
## Why this shape

You stopped Thursday's session because the Achilles got sharper with pace, and Saturday it was stiff for a mile before settling. That is the classic early-warning pattern and the right response is a short, soft week — not a lost block. The race is nine weeks out and your aerobic base is in good shape, so losing a sharpening week costs you nothing.

Quality is out this week. Pace changes and push-off load the Achilles the most, and that is exactly what provoked it. We hold easy aerobic running at flat routes only, and skip the Thursday hill loop.

## How to run this week

Use a simple traffic-light rule each day. Pain under 2/10 that eases in the first mile and does not get worse while running: go. Pain 3/10 or climbing during the run: stop and walk home. Any sharp pain, swelling, or morning limp: do not run and get it looked at.

Shoes stay in the Ghost 16 all week — more stack, less heel drop stress than the Speed 4. Skip calf raises and anything that loads the Achilles hard until a professional clears you. Short, gentle walking is fine and helpful.

## What's next

If the Achilles settles cleanly by Sunday, next week we rebuild to a normal easy week and then layer quality back in the week after. If it is still grumbling, we hold easy or cross-train longer. Nine weeks is enough runway to protect this and still run 3:30 — pushing through it now is what turns a tight tendon into a six-week problem.

answers.question: Should I stop running for a few days, or keep going with easy runs?
answers.answer:
Easy running is okay this week **only** if the Achilles behaves. Use this rule each run:

| Pain during run | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Under 2/10, eases after first mile | Continue as planned |
| 3/10 or climbing | Stop and walk home |
| Sharp, or morning limp next day | Do not run, rest and get it assessed |

I would also take Thursday as a second rest day this week to give it an extra 48-hour window. No pace changes, no hills, no strides. Short walks and gentle ankle mobility are fine. If two consecutive runs feel clean, we are on track to rebuild next week.

answers.question: How do I know if this is serious?
answers.answer:
That is a question for a sports physio, not me — and I would book one this week rather than wait. I can't diagnose anything, but the pattern coaches watch for is: pain that sharpens with pace, morning stiffness that takes more than a few steps to clear, visible swelling or a lump on the tendon, pain when you press it, or pain going up stairs or doing a single-leg calf raise. Any of those earn a visit.

The reassuring signs are: tightness that eases within the first mile of easy running, no morning limp, no swelling, and settles with a day or two off. You are in a mixed picture right now, which is why we train conservatively and get professional eyes on it.

safetyCallouts.title: Get the Achilles assessed this week
safetyCallouts.body:
Pain that sharpens with pace and lingers as morning stiffness is worth a professional look, not a wait-and-see. Please book a sports physio or sports medicine doctor in the next few days — they can tell you what's going on and what loading is safe.

Stop running and seek same-day care if you get sudden sharp pain, a pop or snap sensation, visible swelling, or you can't push off the foot normally. I'm coaching the training around this; the medical read needs to come from a qualified professional.

answers.answer:
**1. Stop, or keep going with easy runs?**

Easy, flat running is okay this week **only if** the Achilles stays at a 3/10 or less, does not sharpen with pace, and is not worse the next morning. Use the first mile as the test: if it eases as you warm up, continue at easy effort. If it stays sore, gets sharper, or you find yourself altering your stride, stop and walk home. No tempo, no hills, no strides until it is quiet for a full week.

**2. How do you know if it is serious?**

I cannot diagnose this, and that is exactly why I would get a sports physio or sports doctor to put hands on it in the next few days rather than wait. Signs that push it from a grumble toward something you need checked urgently:

| Sign | What it looks like |
| --- | --- |
| Sharp or stabbing pain | Not a dull tightness, a clear point of pain |
| Pain that worsens during a run | Starts at 2/10, climbs to 5+/10 |
| Morning pain | Stiff and sore for more than the first few steps, lingers past a mile of walking |
| Swelling or a lump | Any visible thickening of the tendon, or warmth |
| Limping | You change how you walk or run to protect it |
| Pain squeezing the tendon | Pinching it between finger and thumb reproduces the pain |

Any of those, stop running and get it looked at. The 3:30 at Lakeshore is still on the table from a fitness standpoint; it is only off the table if you train through a tendon that is telling you to stop.

new.analysis:
## Why this shape

The tempo on Thursday is the pivot point. HR drifted 36 bpm across four miles, you stopped at three, and the tendon was still talking to you on Saturday and after Sunday. That is not a week to add stimulus — it is a week to remove it and see what the tendon does with calm, flat, easy miles.

## What I kept and what I cut

I kept five run days because walking away entirely tends to make people anxious and does not help the tendon more than easy flat running does, provided it stays quiet. I cut the Thursday quality session, moved it off the hills, and dropped the Sunday long run from a build to a flat 10. Total lands near 28 – 30 miles, roughly matching last week, with none of the sharp edges.

## The good news underneath

Your easy pace has moved from 9:41 to 9:22 at the same 144 HR over four weeks, which is a real aerobic gain and does not disappear in a quiet week. We have nine weeks to the race; losing a quality session now costs almost nothing compared to pushing through a tendon issue and losing a month.

## What next week looks like

If the Achilles is fully quiet by Sunday — no morning stiffness, no stiffness after the long run, no pinch-test pain — we add a short set of marathon-pace miles back on Thursday and nudge the long run to 13. If it is not quiet, we hold flat again and I want to hear what the physio said before we plan any pace work.

safetyCallouts.body: Please book a sports physio or sports doctor in the next few days rather than wait for the weekend. Tendons tend to reward early attention and punish delay. Stop running immediately if you get sharp pain, pain that worsens during a run, swelling, a visible lump, or you start altering your stride.
